To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the adoption and use patterns of stoves are affected by the social and cultural perceptions of users, and that the functional, social and cultural needs of users must be considered when designing stoves.

1) ICSs in rural Guatemala serve multiple purposes beyond cooking food, 2) ICS designs that sacrifice these other uses are less likely to be used, and 3) ICSs should be designed to account for these multiple purposes to increase adoption rates.
improved cookstoves have several layers of practical value beyond cooking food.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social and cultural aspects of ICS adoption and use.
rethinking the diffusion of ICSs by reorienting the focus of stove adoption programs from macro-level “tripling benefits” toward micro-level consumer-centric functional benefits.
how the “triple benefit” paradigm of ICS adoption programs is perceived and used by rural communities in developing countries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the diffusion of improved cookstove programs should be rethought in order to account for social perceptions and cooking needs of the adopters.
the adoption and use patterns of ICSs are not as simple as the “triple benefit” paradigm would suggest.
improved cookstove adoption programs should be rethought to include the social perceptions of users, and the functional needs of users.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stove adoption programs should be designed with an understanding that stoves are not just cooking tools, but also social and cultural objects that are used for a variety of purposes.

the “triple benefit” paradigm is too narrow to account for the full range of social perceptions and uses of ICSs, and therefore should be broadened to account for the functional, social, cultural, and environmental benefits of ICSs in the context of rural communities in Guatemala.
stove programs need to be more culturally and socially relevant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
stove adoption and use decisions are complex and cannot be reduced to a single variable.
stove programs should be more user-centric and less technology-centric.
stove adoption programs must be designed to address the needs of the users.
